meta.title: Aligning Human Oversight in Aerospace: A Cross-Sector Approach to Operationalized Trustworthy AI
meta.authorsHtml: Sofia Kyrampalidou<sup>∗</sup><sup>1</sup>, Tim Robin Kosack<sup>1</sup>, Dr. Simon Odrowski<sup>1</sup>
meta.copyright: © 2026 S. Kyrampalidou et al., licenced via CC BY 4.0.
meta.venue: Proceedings of the 3rd Conference on AI in and for Space (SPAICE 2026)

abstract: Safety-critical space operations increasingly rely on AIenabled decision-support systems to manage conjunction and support collision-avoidance decisions in congested aerospace environments. However, teams still lack guidance on what “human oversight” for high-risk AI systems should look like in an operational setting and in a way that is tangible and auditable. This paper explores a proposed minimum set of sociotechnical oversight actions and their corresponding auditable evidence for demonstrating alignment with the EU AI Act’s requirement on human oversight. Using structured document analysis, we combine the AI Act as a regulatory anchor, EASA guidance as a mature aviation baseline, space operational sources from ESA and NASA and human-factors literature on known oversight failure modes. We propose: (i) a catalogue of oversight actions across the system’s lifecycle (before/during/after an action) and (ii) a Minimum Oversight Evidence Set (MOES) that makes those actions implementable and auditable. A collision avoidance use case walkthrough is used to illustrate how the framework can be applied across both sectors, providing a reusable template for operationalizing trustworthy AI oversight.

blocks.html: More and more AI-enabled decision-support systems are being adopted in aerospace safety-critical operations: from space missions that deal with collision avoidance [1] in congested orbital environments [2] to aviation settings that depend on reliable human-AI teaming [3] [4]. When these systems are introduced, the challenges that arise with them are not only technical in nature but they also raise the question of how the overall sociotechnical system of which they are now a part (technical components, people, procedures, etc.) can actually work safely and effectively in a real-world application [5]. For example, if we think about AI-enabled prediction of re-entry of objects (uncontrolled or planned), estimates with high uncertainty can directly trigger short-notice aerospace restrictions and have an important impact on civil aviation safety. In these cases, how should such a system be designed so that humans can actually interpret the risk, justify the decision taken and handle escalation in an appropriate manner?

Within such settings, “human oversight” could serve as the mechanism that can keep autonomy aligned with safety goals [6]. The EU AI Act (AIA) is also based on this perception, as it requires high-risk AI systems to adopt human oversight measures (Art. 14) in order to mitigate or prevent risks in use [7]. However, the AIA, being a regulatory text, remains intentionally general: it guides organizations towards the route of effective oversight but it does not directly suggest explicit operational measures to be adopted that are going to be auditable. As a result, this paper asks: what is a proposed minimum set of sociotechnical oversight actions and auditable evidence that can demonstrate AIA-aligned human oversight in safety-critical aerospace missions?

We respond to this question with two main results: (i) an “oversight actions” catalogue that shows what meaningful oversight should enable before/during/after an action in a safety-critical setting and (ii) a Minimum Oversight Evidence Set (MOES) that defines a minimum set of evidence that can be used to review whether these actions are actually in place. In this setting, the use of “minimum” refers to coverage of the proposed oversight actions and not to a legal requirement or universally validated standard.

In order to audit and demonstrate human oversight, the first step would be to try to operationalize it into practical measures that can be implemented and reviewed. To do so, we used structured document analysis to derive a set of oversight actions and their associated evidence. The analysis combines four complementary source groups: (1) the AIA as the regulatory anchor for human oversight, (2) European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) AI guidance as a mature sociotechnical baseline from aviation, (3) European Space Agency (ESA) and National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) operational material to ground and adapt the baseline to space operations and collision avoidance and (4) human factors literature to cross-check known oversight failure modes and traceability needs. Documents were selected based on their relevance to human oversight, AI-enabled operational decision support, safety-critical operations and governance or auditability, as well as their authority and currency within the respective domain. The objective was not an exhaustive systematic review, but a structured cross-sector review of key sources relevant to operationalizing human oversight.

The AIA serves as the starting point of the analysis. For systems falling within its high-risk classification, Art. 14 establishes the principal human oversight requirement and is considered together with requirements on risk management (Art. 9), technical documentation (Art. 11), logging (Art. 12), transparency (Art. 13) and robustness (Art. 15) [7]. These requirements were used to identify the main aspects of human oversight that need to become operational and auditable.

Aviation is then used as the initial reference domain because it is an interconnected safety-critical sector [8] [9] that has long experience in supervising automated systems with strict safety constraints [10] [11] and that has also published AI-specific guidance on the matter. EASA has published the EASA Artificial Intelligence Roadmap 2.0, which follows a human-centric approach to trustworthy AI [12] and the EASA AI Concept Paper (three issues), which discusses systems that can take decisions under human oversight [13]. These sources were used to translate the AIA’s high-level requirements into more concrete operational measures and to identify possible oversight actions.

This initial aviation baseline was then adapted to space context. We do not claim that aviation oversight measures are directly transferable to space. Space operations face certain human oversight constraints that are less prominent in aviation (such as latency, connectivity or limited real-time intervention) [14]. ESA and NASA operational material was therefore used to assess whether the identified oversight actions remained relevant and how they would need to be adapted under space-specific conditions. For example, where direct human intervention was less feasible, the focus was shifted towards an oversight-bydesign approach that is embedded in system architecture or procedures – an approach that was more space-fitting.

Finally, human factors literature was used to cross-check the derived oversight actions and evidence against well known oversight and supervision failure modes. This helped assess whether the proposed actions addressed realistic risks associated with human oversight (e.g., overreliance or automation bias), rather than simply trying to meet regulatory requirements.

The final oversight actions were derived through a qualitative assessment across these four source groups. The actions that were considered were relevant to the regulatory text, appeared recurrently across the sources, were operationally important in a safety-critical setting and were applicable across both sectors (aviation and space). Frequency was used only as a sign of agreement across the sources, rather than a strict rule, as an oversight requirement found in one strong source could still be important. These were then grouped into the before/during/after oversight phases presented in Section 3. Where aviation and space sources differed in operational needs, the core oversight requirement was kept, but the action was adapted to fit the specific operational context.

For each selected action, we then asked what evidence would allow an internal reviewer or an external auditor to confirm that the action was carried out. This evidence was selected based on how directly they were relevant to the action, how easy they were to audit and how clearly they demonstrated oversight. When multiple evidence items served the same purpose, they were combined to avoid repetition. These were later organized into the seven MOES categories presented in Section 4, which together support the eight proposed oversight actions.

The list below serves as a catalogue of oversight actions that makes human oversight operational by describing what must be in place before, during and after an action in a safety-critical decision-support setting. To derive the catalogue, we used the AIA’s Art. 14 on human oversight and translated it into concrete possible action points by utilizing EASA’s AI baseline and then adjusting it to human oversight under space-specific restraints. Human factors literature on human oversight/supervision failures (e.g., human out-of-the-loop [15], automation bias or complacency [16]) was used in order to check whether the actions really address realistic needs in a high-pressure and uncertain scenario (keeping collision avoidance always in mind).

How to read the catalogue: the catalogue is not a specific domain procedure, but rather a list of oversight actions that should be implemented to enable meaningful human oversight. Each action can then be adapted to each domain with certain triggers/thresholds (e.g., intervention levels might significantly differ between the sectors).

blocks.title: Result II: Minimum oversight evidence set (MOES)

blocks.html: The MOES list is the second result of our analysis and it showcases a set of concrete evidence that should be kept in order for the involved teams to ensure that human oversight is feasible and actually implementable in their operations. Our guiding question here was “what would an internal reviewer or an external auditor like to see in order to say that this human oversight action is indeed in place and used?”. This approach aligns well with the AIA’s logic (Art. 14 – Human Oversight in combination with Art. 9, 11–13, 15).

“Minimum” does not mean that the seven evidence elements constitute a legally instructed and exhaustive validated compliance set. Rather, together they provide evidence covering all eight proposed oversight actions. There is no strict one-to-one relationship between actions and evidence. One evidence element could support multiple oversight actions where the information is closely relevant. Depending on the system and operational context additional evidence may therefore be required.

How to read the MOES list: MOES identifies the evidence considered necessary to demonstrate the proposed oversight actions. The exact form in which this evidence is documented may differ across organizations and sectors.
E1 Oversight ConOps (supports A1, A6, A8)
• ConOps/task allocation document that lists end users, roles, responsibilities and how tasks are allocated across HMI teams (CO-01, CO-04). [13]
• Roles+responsibilities section in collision-avoidance workflow documentation. [17] Possible evidence forms: documents, process maps E2 Safe-use conditions+no-use specs (supports A2, A4, A6)
• OD/ODD+limitations/assumptions documented as part of ConOps. [13]
• Operational thresholds+timing constraints (e.g., collision probability, GO/NOGO timing). [19]
• Screening “safety volume/protective volume” parameters+escalation to risk assessment/mitigation. [17]

• Assumptions/limits tied to uncertainty models (e.g., timevarying uncertainty, Gaussian/limitations). [20] Possible evidence forms: documents, configuration files, checklists E3 Operator output+UI specs (supports A4, A6)
• Operator-facing explainability (what is shown+timing). [13]
• HMI/interaction description (e.g., monitoring/override controls). [13]
• Explainable AI requirement statement for CA decisionmaking. [20] ups/screenshots, user guides, explanation/uncertain specs on display E4 Intervention feasibility plan (space) (supports A5, A2)

• Maneuver feasibility/timing constraints (prep/execute time, GO/NOGO decision timing). [19]

• Training syllabus+recurrent training plan (AI basics, HF, explainability, safety/security topics). [13]
• Training assessment evidence (theory+practical assessment). [19]

• Known issues as training justifications (e.g., complacency, automation bias, misuse). [15] [16] [21] Possible evidence forms: training syllabus, attendance records, assessment results, simulations E7 Post-event review+learning pack (supports A8, A7, A1)
• Continuous safety assessment/in-service monitoring artefacts (ORG-03). [13]
• “Lessons learnt”+periodic reporting extracted from tickets/task allocation outputs, including assigned responsibilities. [19]

• Corrective actions+recommendations follow-up records. [22] Possible evidence forms: ticket logs, incident reports, lessons learnt notes, metrics dashboards, corrective action trackers, closure status lists [22]

blocks.title: Use case walkthrough and discussion (collision avoidance as a bridge)

blocks.html: With this section, we would like to showcase how the oversight actions catalogue and the MOES list can be applied in a collision avoidance scenario. The walkthrough is kept intentionally light, as its purpose is to show when oversight actions and MOES can actually be realized in a real workflow, rather than to define a complete collision avoidance procedure. The main aim is to demonstrate operational applicability and traceability between the proposed actions and their corresponding evidence, rather than to empirically test whether the framework reduces oversight failures or improves operational outcomes.

Before action: in both aviation and space, collision avoidance starts with clear definition of authority and escalation logic (A1, E1) [13] [18] [19]. Before any action, the involved teams need to decide who is allowed to accept/reject/modify a recommendation and who/what can trigger an escalation. The safe-use conditions and no-use triggers (A2, E2) then define when AI outputs are valid and could be relied upon (e.g., uncertainty rates). This is of special value in congested aerospace environments where alerts or updates might be frequent and the operator might be under time pressure. Training (A3, E6) assists the operators with dealing with unknown situations or common oversight/supervision pitfalls, such as over-reliance on or over-trust in the system in its decision-support outputs [16] [21].

During action: in time- and safety-critical situations, failures might arise not only from the absence of a humanin-the-loop, but also from the lack of meaningful oversight [23] [24]. This is why we included in the catalogue: the need for transparency when it comes to decision-relevant information and for feasible intervention when deemed needed (A5, E4). During a collision avoidance decision, operators need outputs that support action planning and commitment (rather than mere recommendations) [25] [17]. However, in order to be able to meaningfully rely on those outputs, information like uncertainty levels or next-step options must also be provided. As mentioned before, human oversight in a space setting cannot always take the form of real-time manual control, but it is better to follow an oversight-by-design approach. For this reason, aspects like autonomy bounds or safe modes in case of errors should be clearly defined and reported (A5, E4). Finally, alert triage and escalation points (A6, E1, E3) are focused on addressing workload. The workflow should seamlessly integrate additional human review for the cases that are most safetycritical and also prevent rubber-stamping when alerts are flooding the system.

After action: both the aviation and space sectors have a long history in reconstructing accidents, incidents and near-misses by recording all evidence that could assist a post-action investigation [22] [26]. Especially when it comes to AI-enabled systems, auditability becomes more concrete when the system’s activity is recorded (as also instructed by the AIA, Art. 12) so events/decisions can be thoroughly traced and reconstructed after the action has taken place. Traceability and reconstruction (A7, E5) ensure this is met. By knowing what the inputs, model version, outputs, human actions and thresholds were, one can reconstruct a decision end-to-end and pinpoint the successes and the failures of the action. Post-action review (A8, E7) then uses this evidence to identify lessons learnt, incidents requiring follow-up, corrective actions and safety recommendations. The same evidence also shows who is responsible for each action and whether it has been completed or not. This links back to the roles and decision authority defined in A1. This closes the loop between operational experience and the oversight measures used in future operations.

Further discussion: collision avoidance serves as a useful indicative bridge for both sectors as it poses the operators with similar oversight challenges, such as timepressure and uncertainty. At the same time though, the proposed actions and MOES are not just specific to collision avoidance. Any safety-critical AI-enabled decisionsupport setting with similar supervision/oversight risks (e.g., workload or uncertainty) can reuse the same structure, by then adapting the domain-specific triggers, metrics and processes.

This paper proposes a compact way to make human oversight operational and auditable in safety-critical aerospace decision-support settings, with a small reusable template that can be used across aerospace teams. The first contribution is an oversight actions catalogue which clarifies what must be enabled and highlighted for meaningful oversight. The second contribution is MOES, which is a minimum set of oversight evidence that the involved teams should have at hand (e.g., in the form of a document or applied measure) in order to demonstrate that they apply meaningful human oversight in practice. The overall approach connects a regulatory anchor (AI Act) with a mature sociotechnical baseline of human-AI teaming from aviation (EASA) and a space-specific operational grounding (ESA, NASA).

This cross-sector approach is valuable as aviation and space have long collaborated closely with each other, sharing common safety cultures, tools or governance practices. The reuse of compatible material can help reduce duplication of work and improve alignment, making oversight practices across domains more consistent. Given the fact that the proposed catalogue and MOES were derived from structured document analysis, future work around this could include validation of the proposed actions and evidence with input received from space operations and human factors practitioners and/or testing whether they indeed reduce oversight failure modes under realistic workload or uncertainty. This validation can turn the template into a concrete tool that will assist teams with operationalizing oversight in a way that is already demanded by EU regulation and that can be audited without reinventing governance practices each time.
